problem: 'can ever be sanctioned' became 'will ever sanction' (can to will)
replacement: In America conscription is unknown, and men are persuaded to enlist by bounties. The ideas and habits of the people of the United States are so opposed to compulsory enlistment that I do not think it can ever be sanctioned by the laws. What the French call the conscription is certainly the heaviest tax on the population of that country; yet how could a great continental war be fought without it? The Americans have not adopted the British practice of pressing seamen into service, and they have nothing like the French system of maritime conscription. The navy, like the merchant service, is staffed by volunteers. But it is hard to see how a nation could sustain a great naval war without resorting to one or the other of these two systems. Indeed, the Union, which has fought with some distinction at sea, has never had a very large fleet, and equipping the small number of American ships has always been extremely expensive.

Another cause tends to make the efforts of a democratic government less persevering than those of an aristocracy. The lower classes are not only less alert than the higher orders to the good or bad chances of the future, but they also suffer far more keenly from present privations. The nobleman does risk his life, but the chance of glory is as great as the chance of harm. If he gives up a large part of his income to the State, he deprives himself for a time of the pleasures of wealth. But for the poor man, death is adorned with no pomp or renown, and the taxes that are irksome to the rich are fatal to him.

problem: 'rude manners' (moeurs) rendered 'rough manners'; STYLE-NOTE manners/customs rule
replacement: In America there is no law against fraudulent bankruptcies. This is not because they are few, but because bankruptcies are so numerous. The fear of being prosecuted as a bankrupt weighs more heavily on the minds of most people than the fear of being dragged into losses or ruin by other people’s failures. And the public conscience extends a kind of guilty tolerance to an offense that everyone condemns as an individual. In the new States of the Southwest, the citizens generally take justice into their own hands, and murders are very frequent. This comes from the rough customs and the ignorance of the inhabitants of those wilderness regions, who do not see the use of giving the law adequate force and who prefer duels to prosecutions.

It is therefore very hard to say, at present, how much sagacity the American democracy will show in conducting the country’s foreign policy. On this point both its adversaries and its advocates must suspend judgment. As for myself, I do not hesitate to state my conviction that it is above all in the conduct of foreign relations that democratic governments seem to me decidedly inferior to governments run on different principles. Experience, instruction, and habit can almost always succeed in giving democracies a kind of practical discretion, and that knowledge of the daily events of life which is called good sense. Good sense may be enough to direct the ordinary course of society, and among a people whose education has been provided for, the advantages of democratic liberty in the country’s internal affairs may more than make up for the evils inherent in a democratic government. But this is not always so in the relations between foreign nations.
